issues.detail: The primary action promises an availability check and the header promises “RENT ONLINE,” but the supporting microcopy states that availability and final rental terms are confirmed later via WhatsApp. The scan also records zero booking signals. This turns what appears to be a transactional journey into an opaque manual enquiry without setting expectations clearly enough.
issues.evidence: Hero form reads “CHECK AVAILABILITY”; desktop header reads “RENT ONLINE”; hero support text says “Direct enquiry. Availability and final rental terms are confirmed with Mfinity via WhatsApp.” Objective scan: bookingSignalCount 0, contactSignalCount 4.
issues.expected: A reference luxury-rental flow distinguishes instant booking from concierge enquiry and gives the customer a clear, credible next step: dates, selected vehicle, price basis, availability state, and the resulting reservation or concierge action.
issues.location: Desktop and mobile hero booking module; top navigation CTA
issues.observed: The page uses booking language but discloses a manual WhatsApp confirmation only after the form, creating a capability and expectation mismatch at the most important conversion point.
issues.recommendation: Either implement a real reservation/availability path with an explicit result state, or relabel the experience consistently as “Request availability” or “Speak to a concierge.” Carry selected dates and vehicle into the next step, state response timing, and make the outcome of submission explicit.
issues.title: Transactional promise does not match the actual enquiry flow

issues.detail: The luxury positioning is visually asserted but not substantively supported at the decision point. There are no visible reassurance signals around deposits, insurance, verified fleet ownership/condition, delivery coverage, cancellation, ratings, or concierge service standards.
issues.evidence: Objective scan reports trustSignalCount 0. The desktop vehicle panel only shows “Deposit €7,000 · longer stays on request”; mobile hero shows no trust or service proof near the form.
issues.expected: Reference-quality premium rental sites earn permission to enquire through concise, specific proof: fully insured terms, delivery areas, service hours, transparent deposit framing, verified reviews, and real operational credentials.
issues.location: Hero availability module and vehicle pricing/reservation area
issues.observed: A high-ticket decision is asked for before the site establishes why Mfinity is a credible and low-friction operator in Marbella.
issues.recommendation: Add a compact, concrete reassurance strip adjacent to the conversion path, plus fuller rental assurances on vehicle detail and checkout/enquiry screens. Use operational facts rather than generic luxury claims.
issues.title: No trust layer around a high-consideration rental enquiry

issues.detail: The mobile first viewport makes the customer work through a large form before they can inspect a specific available car, price, or meaningful vehicle choice. The featured Ferrari availability panel visible on desktop is absent from the mobile composition shown.
issues.evidence: Mobile screenshot dedicates the lower half of the screen to date fields, vehicle selector, and a full-width action; it shows “Any Mfinity car” rather than a car, rate, or availability result. Desktop screenshot presents a Ferrari 488 Spyder panel with €1,400/day and “Reserve now.”
issues.expected: On mobile, luxury vehicle discovery should remain visual and decisive: lead with a chosen car or a scannable inventory entry, then make date-led availability filtering easy without obscuring the product.
issues.observed: The compact desktop merchandising composition becomes a form-heavy mobile screen with little product proof or pricing context.
issues.recommendation: Preserve a featured-car card or visible inventory preview on mobile, ideally with image, vehicle name, from-price, and availability CTA. Keep date selection available, but make it a compact filter or a progressive next step rather than the dominant first-screen experience.
issues.title: Mobile prioritizes the form over vehicle discovery

issues.detail: The hero image is heavily blurred across most of both viewports. While the red Ferrari provides color and motion, the actual premium vehicle is cropped tightly and not inspectable; the background reads more like an atmospheric stock treatment than evidence of a luxury fleet.
issues.evidence: Both supplied screenshots show substantial deliberate blur over trees, architecture, and much of the vehicle. On mobile the Ferrari is cropped through the middle/lower screen, with no full-car view; objective scan reports only 6 images across the page.
issues.expected: Cinematic does not mean visually withholding. A reference luxury rental site uses art direction to show unmistakable, sharp vehicle forms, material quality, and the Marbella setting, especially before the customer is asked to convert.
issues.observed: The hero achieves mood, but sacrifices product legibility and some perceived authenticity. The single visual has to carry both brand and fleet proof, and it does not fully do so.
issues.recommendation: Use a sharp, intentional hero frame that reveals the full vehicle or a clearly recognizable detail, with a restrained overlay for text contrast. Support it with consistent, editorial-quality vehicle photography in the collection rather than relying on blur to create luxury atmosphere.
issues.title: Cinematic treatment obscures the product

issues.detail: The desktop conversion hierarchy competes with itself: “Explore collection,” the date form’s “Check availability,” and the Ferrari card’s “Reserve now” all present plausible primary actions, while the header adds “Rent online.” The vehicle card’s availability and price are not visibly connected to the date input.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot contains four prominent action labels in the hero: “RENT ONLINE,” “EXPLORE COLLECTION,” “CHECK AVAILABILITY,” and “RESERVE NOW.” Objective scan records 4 primary CTAs and an inconsistentButtonRatio of 0.3404.
issues.expected: A premium booking surface has one dominant task per state. Vehicle discovery, date selection, and reservation should connect into a single obvious sequence, with secondary paths visually quieter.
issues.location: Desktop hero navigation, left-side content/form, and right-side featured vehicle card
issues.observed: The page has several conversion invitations but no clearly dominant route or visible handoff between the form and featured vehicle reservation.
issues.recommendation: Choose a primary hero journey, such as select dates then view matching cars. Make secondary exploration a lower-emphasis link. When a featured vehicle is shown, connect its reserve action to date selection and clarify whether its displayed daily price applies to the selected dates.
issues.title: Competing hero CTAs dilute the booking path

issues.detail: The brand voice has strong short-form rhythm, but several key headings are generic lifestyle copy rather than useful rental decision content. “Luxury in every kilometer,” “Keep the feeling,” and “at full volume” do little to clarify fleet breadth, booking conditions, delivery, or why Mfinity is distinctive in Puerto Banús.
issues.evidence: Heading samples include “Luxury in every kilometer.”, “A collection built for Marbella at full volume.” and “Choose the car. Keep the feeling.” The page has 638 words, but no measured trust signals and no booking signal.
issues.expected: Luxury copy should be spare but information-rich: it should pair mood with verifiable reasons to choose the operator and reduce the questions that block an enquiry.
issues.observed: The language establishes a recognizable luxury-car template tone but does not yet create a differentiated, locally authoritative proposition.
issues.recommendation: Retain the concise editorial tone while replacing some slogan-level copy with specific value: Puerto Banús/Marbella delivery, vehicle categories, concierge availability, insurance/deposit clarity, and how the enquiry process works.
issues.title: Copy favors luxury mood over differentiated decision support

issues.detail: The main mobile action target is marginally undersized for a critical touch interaction, and the header’s “RENT ONLINE” label is slightly below the scan’s readable-text threshold. These are minor defects, but below the polish expected of a premium mobile booking surface.
issues.evidence: Objective scan identifies “EXPLORE COLLECTION” at 169.1 x 38px as the sole tiny tap target and “RENT ONLINE” at 11.8px as the sole tiny-text instance.
issues.expected: Critical mobile actions should comfortably meet at least 44px touch height, with compact navigation labels still clearly legible and consistent with the brand type scale.
issues.location: Mobile hero “EXPLORE COLLECTION” control; desktop/mobile navigation booking CTA
issues.observed: The UI is generally responsive and clean, but these two controls fall just below the expected physical and typographic comfort level.
issues.recommendation: Increase the explore control hit area to 44px minimum without changing its visual weight, and raise the navigation CTA label to a clearly readable minimum while retaining the current tracking and spacing system.
issues.title: Two critical controls are slightly under-crafted for mobile

aiReview.summary: Mfinity is a polished, high-performing luxury-rental concept with strong first-impression art direction and unusually solid responsive technical execution. It is not yet reference quality for the real booking business: the product imagery is too withheld, the mobile first screen is form-heavy, the reservation promise resolves into an unclear manual enquiry, and there is virtually no trust evidence around a high-value rental. The highest-value improvement is to make one date-to-vehicle-to-enquiry/reservation path explicit, credible, and product-led.
strengths: The hero has immediate category recognition: a performance car, Marbella locator, refined dark treatment, and restrained navigation establish the intended luxury-rental context quickly.
The desktop layout has a strong editorial composition, balancing the headline, availability form, and featured-vehicle panel without visible clutter.
Typography is generally confident and legible at display scale, and the hierarchy from location marker to headline to booking area is clear.
Responsive execution is structurally solid: the scan reports no horizontal overflow, zero mobile CLS, working forms, no failed requests, and excellent loading metrics.
The site provides clear basic contact routes, legal/privacy access, descriptive image alternatives, and a sensible heading outline.

issues.detail: The primary business task is visiting a physical cafe, but the home page does not make the practical visit decision possible above the fold or in the scanned page signals. “MARBELLA · SPAIN” establishes only a broad destination; no street address, map/directions, phone number, or opening hours are surfaced. The scan also records no booking signal and shows email/contact links rather than an immediate visit utility.
issues.evidence: Desktop and mobile screenshots show only the broad location label and “VISÍTANOS HOY”; the DOM scan records bookingSignalCount: 0. Contact signals are limited to the Contacto page and mailto link.
issues.expected: A reference premium hospitality site turns intent into action with precise location, current hours, and a map/directions route at the point the visitor is persuaded to come.
issues.location: Home hero, particularly the “VISÍTANOS HOY” secondary CTA and lower visit-information area
issues.observed: The visit CTA is visually present but is unsupported by the practical information required to decide when and where to visit.
issues.recommendation: Make “Visítanos” lead to, or reveal, a concise visit module with full Puerto Banús address, today’s hours, tap-to-call, and a prominent “Cómo llegar” map/deep-link. Keep this reachable within the first scroll on mobile.
issues.title: Visit CTA lacks actionable location and hours

issues.detail: The hero assigns the strongest visual weight to menu discovery, while the stated primary goal is visit/contact. “DESCUBRIR LA CARTA” is a large filled button, whereas “VISÍTANOS HOY” is only a light text link with an underline. This makes the secondary journey the apparent primary conversion action.
issues.evidence: In both screenshots, the menu CTA is a large high-contrast rectangular control. The visit CTA is text-only and visually subordinate despite being the critical journey.
issues.expected: The hierarchy should reflect the business objective: visit/directions or contact should be the dominant action, with menu exploration a clear but secondary route.
issues.location: Hero CTA group on desktop and mobile
issues.observed: Menu exploration is easier to notice and tap than the route most likely to produce an in-person visit.
issues.recommendation: Elevate “Visítanos” or “Cómo llegar” to the primary button treatment, and retain Carta as a secondary outlined or text treatment. On mobile, include a directions icon or map cue to make the outcome explicit.
issues.title: Hero CTA hierarchy favors the secondary goal

issues.detail: The page looks polished and venue-led, but it under-delivers on product proof for a premium sugar-free patisserie. The hero image is dominated by the counter, fittings, and ceiling; individual pastries are small behind reflective glass. On mobile, the crop becomes even more interior-led, with the product selection difficult to inspect.
issues.evidence: The only supplied desktop and mobile views use the same wide cafe-interior image. Visible pastries occupy a small, partially obscured portion of the display case. The scan reports only 8 images across the page.
issues.expected: For an appetite-led premium patisserie, the first visual sequence should make crafted products legible: texture, finish, portions, and plated selection should be visible at editorial quality alongside venue context.
issues.location: Home hero image, especially the mobile crop
issues.observed: The space communicates an upscale cafe, but the actual sugar-free patisserie offer is not visually persuasive enough to distinguish it from a generic premium coffee venue.
issues.recommendation: Use a mobile-specific hero crop or image that keeps a signature pastry and drink clearly visible, then introduce close, well-lit editorial product photography immediately below the fold. Retain venue photography as supporting proof rather than the sole hero asset.
issues.title: Hero imagery is stronger for venue mood than product appetite

issues.detail: The language treatment feels unresolved: navigation and supporting copy are predominantly Spanish, while the central proposition is English (“No sugar. Same taste.”); desktop also presents “PÂTISSERIE & CAFÉ” and “MARBELLA · SPAIN.” The ES / EN control is visible, but the shown Spanish state remains materially mixed.
issues.evidence: The screenshots simultaneously show “CONCEPTO,” “CARTA,” “VISÍTANOS,” and “DESCUBRIR LA CARTA” with the English H1 and English location label. The document language is Spanish (lang: es).
issues.expected: A bilingual luxury hospitality site can use a foreign-language brand line deliberately, but the reading language of navigational and explanatory content should be internally consistent and the language control should produce a complete, intentional locale.
issues.observed: The mixture can read as decorative international styling rather than a deliberate bilingual content system, slightly reducing clarity and brand precision.
issues.recommendation: Choose a canonical Spanish home-page voice and localize the hero proposition, or make the English phrase an explicitly secondary campaign line. Ensure ES and EN each switch the full interface and body copy consistently.
issues.title: Mixed Spanish and English weakens editorial coherence

issues.detail: The sugar-free promise is stated confidently, but no visible credibility marker supports a health-adjacent premium claim. The scan records zero trust signals, while the proposition asks guests to accept that traditional indulgence is possible “sin azúcar” without further proof.
issues.evidence: The hero says “No sugar. Same taste.” and describes a more conscious way to enjoy sweets. Objective scan: trustSignalCount: 0.
issues.expected: Reference execution supports a differentiated product claim with concise, credible signals: maker expertise, ingredient philosophy, relevant dietary clarification, press/guest proof, or product-specific detail without overloading the page.
issues.location: Hero proposition and concept section entry
issues.observed: The claim is memorable but currently functions more as a slogan than substantiated premium positioning.
issues.recommendation: Add a restrained proof layer below the hero, such as Eric’s credentials, a clear statement of what “sin azúcar” means, ingredient/creation standards, and selected third-party or customer validation where available.
issues.title: Core sugar-free claim has no visible proof layer

issues.detail: The compact mobile header uses a text-heavy outlined Contacto button alongside the language toggle and menu icon. It consumes a substantial portion of the top row and competes with the Zùsto wordmark, while the important “café by Eric” endorsement visible on desktop is omitted.
issues.evidence: In the mobile screenshot, “CONTACTO” is a large pill-shaped control between “ES / EN” and the hamburger, and the logo is reduced to “ZÙSTO.” Desktop retains “café by Eric.”
issues.expected: A premium mobile header should preserve brand meaning and provide a calm, efficient route to the key action without crowding the first visual impression.
issues.observed: The header feels mechanically adapted from desktop rather than independently composed for a narrow, image-led first screen.
issues.recommendation: Use a compact contact/directions icon with an accessible label, or move contact prominence into the hero CTA group. Preserve “by Eric” in the opened navigation or a compact brand lockup, and give the logo more visual ownership.
issues.title: Mobile header crowds the brand lockup

issues.detail: The site uses several competing action treatments: filled rectangular menu CTA, underlined visit link, outlined pill Contacto button, and small uppercase navigation links. The objective scan also finds a 30.8% inconsistent button ratio.
issues.evidence: The desktop and mobile hero/header visibly use three different CTA grammars. Objective scan: inconsistentButtonRatio: 0.3076923076923077.
issues.expected: A premium editorial interface can use primary and secondary treatments, but their semantics should be stable: one treatment for primary conversion, one for secondary navigation, and one quiet utility style.
issues.location: Global header and hero CTA group
issues.observed: The variation dilutes the intended priority system, particularly between contact, menu, and visit actions.
issues.recommendation: Define and apply a concise hierarchy: primary filled action for visit/directions, secondary outlined action for Carta or Contacto, and text links for tertiary navigation. Keep dimensions and arrow usage consistent across those roles.
issues.title: CTA styling lacks a fully consistent hierarchy

aiReview.summary: Zùsto Café presents as an unusually polished, premium editorial cafe site with a clear differentiator and excellent technical execution. It is not yet reference quality for its stated commercial purpose because the home experience makes the menu more prominent than an actual visit, provides too little practical visit information, and relies on venue atmosphere where close product proof and claim credibility are needed. The largest gains are in making the visit path immediately actionable and making the sugar-free patisserie itself more visible and believable.
strengths: The hero has a strong premium hospitality atmosphere: composed venue photography, restrained palette, generous scale, and sophisticated serif/sans-serif contrast avoid generic cafe-site styling.
The proposition is immediate and differentiated. “No sugar. Same taste.” gives the brand a clear, memorable reason to exist before the user has to navigate.
The desktop and mobile layouts retain high legibility over photography, with a strong visual focal point and no evidence of overflow, cramped body copy, or unstable loading behavior.

Navigation, menu discovery, concept, Eric, visit, and contact are all represented in the information architecture; the scan finds no broken internal links, missing image alt text, or console/network failures.
The technical delivery is exceptionally clean, with fast measured loading, negligible layout shift, no blocking time, and strong accessibility/SEO baseline checks.

issues.detail: The mobile hero consumes an unusually long first screen sequence before the visitor reaches any substantive portfolio, solution, proof, or contact content. The duplicated hero detail panel is particularly expensive vertically after two large CTAs.
issues.evidence: In the supplied 780 x 1688 mobile screenshot, the hero still occupies the full view through the project brief and lower divider; the next section is not visible. The scan reports mobile usability at 80, despite no overflow and excellent performance.
issues.expected: A reference-quality mobile landing view would make the proposition and primary enquiry action clear immediately, then reveal the next useful content or proof within the initial browsing flow.
issues.observed: A mobile prospect must scroll through decorative/project metadata before encountering evidence that the company is credible for their use case.
issues.recommendation: Compress the hero after the primary CTA. Move “Ámbito / Base / Modalidad / Enfoque” into a compact expandable proof strip or below the first solution/proof section, and ensure the next section is visibly introduced at the bottom of the first viewport.
issues.title: Mobile landing experience is over-invested in hero presentation

issues.detail: The primary conversion path is repeated as links to a separate contact page, but the homepage presents no form, callback promise, response-time expectation, phone contact, or low-friction enquiry mechanism alongside the intent-building content.
issues.evidence: The scan records two primary CTAs and six contact signals, but zero forms, zero booking signals, and only one trust signal. Both visible CTA buttons use the same “Solicitar presupuesto” destination.
issues.expected: For a high-consideration professional service, visitors should understand what happens after enquiry and be able to begin it with minimal context-switching, backed by practical reassurance.
issues.location: Hero CTA system and homepage conversion path
issues.observed: The page asks for a quote before showing sufficient purchase reassurance, and it offers no visible mechanism to capture high-intent visitors who do not continue to the contact page.
issues.recommendation: Add a short, clearly labelled enquiry module or persistent contact option after the primary services/proof content. State the practical next step and response expectation; expose a telephone/WhatsApp route where appropriate for Spain-based municipal and event enquiries.
issues.title: Lead path lacks reassurance and on-page capture

issues.detail: The hero has a polished editorial art direction, but the combination of oversized serif headline, ultra-small all-caps metadata, hairline rules, numbered “Project brief” panel, and decorative vertical marker reads more like a generic premium-agency template than a transport specialist with established operational credibility.
issues.evidence: Both screenshots show the same highly stylized hero system. The scan also records 35 colors, five font families, and 96 visible tiny-text elements (38% of visible elements).
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution would retain a distinctive brand signature while making the visual language feel native to a real Spanish tourism-mobility operator: confident operational information, authentic fleet/location imagery, and fewer ornamental interface conventions.
issues.observed: The hierarchy privileges aesthetic theatre over proof of service, fleet capability, route expertise, or client confidence.
issues.recommendation: Simplify the ornamental brief/line system; establish one disciplined type system; replace some decorative hero metadata with a concise operational proof point such as service scope, fleet capacity, years operating, or named municipal/event experience.
issues.title: Strong art direction, but a conspicuous template/editorial treatment weakens category authenticity

issues.detail: Small uppercase labels and navigation are pushed below comfortable reading and touch sizes. This is not merely an accessibility detail: it makes a professional services offer feel less legible and less assured.
issues.evidence: The scan finds 96 tiny-text elements, including 7-9.5 px labels, CTA text at 9 px, and navigation at 9.5 px. It also finds 19 tiny interactive targets out of 23, including desktop navigation links only 13 px high.
issues.expected: Reference-quality typography uses small text sparingly and preserves legibility, especially for navigation, CTAs, service labels, and factual information. Controls should have generous hit areas independent of text size.
issues.location: Desktop header, hero kicker, CTA labels, inline links, and project-brief panel
issues.observed: Essential action and navigation language is visually subordinate to the point that it risks being overlooked; the large headline is much better resolved than supporting interaction text.
issues.recommendation: Raise the minimum functional text size and contrast for nav, CTAs, metadata, and inline links. Increase interactive hit areas to at least 44 px high and use fewer all-caps micro-labels; preserve the headline scale without starving the supporting system.
issues.title: Microtypography undermines readability and perceived care

issues.detail: The lead statement clearly identifies tourist trains/trams, but it does not quickly distinguish the offer, decision criteria, or appropriate route by audience. “Cities, events, town halls and venues” is broad segmentation rather than a reason to choose this provider.
issues.evidence: The hero copy is: “Trenes y tranvías turísticos para ciudades, eventos, ayuntamientos y recintos.” The document has 527 words and a services section headed “Cuatro contextos. Una misma exigencia,” but the objective scan finds only one trust signal.
issues.expected: A specialist provider should make audience-specific value concrete: what is delivered, whether it is rental/sale/management, how safety/logistics/route setup are handled, and what credible outcomes or installations demonstrate capability.
issues.location: Homepage hero and early service introduction
issues.observed: The proposition sounds polished but generalized, and the business lacks visible reasons to prefer it over another tourist-train supplier.
issues.recommendation: Introduce a sharper service architecture immediately after the hero: rental, sale, event operation, municipal projects, and management, each with a tangible outcome. Add named client/municipality/event proof, fleet specifications, service geography, and concise case-study results.
issues.title: Positioning is elegant but insufficiently differentiated or evidenced

issues.detail: The interface makes a commercial lead request prominent while omitting visible privacy and legal destinations. For Spanish public-sector, venue, and event buyers, this weakens legitimacy at the point where personal and procurement contact may be initiated.
issues.evidence: The scan reports no privacy link and no legal link, with a security/trust score of 75.4 and only one detected trust signal.
issues.expected: Reference-quality professional services sites visibly provide legal/privacy information and reinforce commercial credibility with company identity, service assurances, and verifiable client or project proof.
issues.observed: There is no detected legal or privacy link despite repeated quote-request CTAs.

The priority is to turn the visual promise into commercial confidence: reduce microtype and hero excess, surface authentic proof and audience-specific service clarity, make mobile progression more efficient, and provide a more reassuring, lower-friction enquiry journey.
strengths: The hero uses a genuinely relevant vehicle image rather than generic stock photography, and the red train plus restrained gold/black palette creates immediate category recognition.
The primary value proposition and quote CTA are visible above the fold on desktop and mobile.
The desktop composition has deliberate alignment, stable spacing, and no evidence of layout shift or horizontal overflow.
The site has a coherent Spanish-language information architecture, valid heading progression, working internal links, and strong measured loading performance.
The mobile CTA buttons are large, clear, and visually separated despite the broader mobile-density issue.

issues.detail: The desktop charter finder is styled as a broad five-field data strip, but its decisive action is visually weak relative to the amount of space allocated to passive selection information. issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot: guests, date, duration, departure and day occupy most of the hero-width control; the action is confined to the far-right dark cell. The mobile version improves prominence with a full-width action, making the desktop disparity evident.
issues.expected: A premium enquiry configurator should make its continuation state unmistakable at a glance, with an obvious primary action and clear affordances for editable fields.
issues.observed: The interface looks polished, but the action hierarchy is closer to an editorial layout than a high-intent booking flow.
issues.recommendation: Increase the visual weight and horizontal allocation of the primary action, remove or subordinate the decorative vertical label, and make all field controls visibly interactive with compact indicators such as chevrons or selectors.
issues.title: Desktop charter finder underweights its primary action

issues.detail: The desktop page has a meaningful layout-stability problem during loading, which can disrupt first impressions and cause visitors to miss or mis-target the hero enquiry control.
issues.evidence: Objective measurement reports desktop CLS of 0.7092, far above the 0.1 good threshold, while mobile CLS is 0. The hero contains large image and booking-panel regions susceptible to late layout changes.
issues.expected: A premium booking interface should hold its composition steady from first paint, particularly around headline, pricing and enquiry controls.
issues.observed: The polished static composition is undermined by visible desktop instability in the primary conversion viewport.

issues.title: Desktop hero suffers severe layout shift

issues.detail: The headline is evocative but generic, while the support line groups private yacht charter, sailing, fishing and group experiences together. This broad framing weakens the exclusive yacht-charter positioning and does not make a clear first-choice proposition for the visitor.

issues.recommendation: Retain the editorial headline, but sharpen the supporting copy around private crewed charters from Puerto Banus and add a concise 'from' price or fleet-led pricing path that explains the VAT/season context before an enquiry is required.
issues.title: Premium proposition and pricing context are too diffuse

issues.detail: Button treatment is not fully systematised: the header uses a soft white pill, the desktop finder action is a dark rectangular text cell, and mobile introduces both a large white rectangular action and outlined WhatsApp action.
issues.evidence: The screenshots show four materially different CTA treatments. The objective scan also reports an inconsistent button ratio of 0.227.
issues.expected: A luxury interface can use primary and secondary actions, but they should share stable typographic, spacing and interaction rules so hierarchy feels intentional rather than page-specific.

issues.recommendation: Define one primary charter-action treatment and one secondary contact treatment, then apply them consistently across header, finder and mobile sticky controls. Use state and prominence, not unrelated shapes, to establish hierarchy.

aiReview.summary: Marbella Boat Charter is materially above the typical yacht-charter template: it has a credible editorial identity, clear discovery routes and a functional enquiry-led journey. It is not reference quality yet because the product is visually absent on the mobile first viewport, desktop conversion hierarchy is too subdued, visible proof is missing for a high-consideration purchase, and the measured desktop layout shift is severe. Resolve these issues while making pricing and proposition more commercially explicit, and the site would support its premium positioning far more convincingly.
strengths: The homepage has a distinctive editorial direction, with a refined serif/display headline against restrained marine imagery rather than a generic booking-site template.
The architecture directly supports the commercial journey: fleet, experiences, destinations, owners, contact and booking are all present, with no broken internal links or journey failure in the scan.

Mobile navigation and conversion treatment are materially clearer than many luxury travel sites: phone contact is visible, the menu target is generous, and the 'Find my charter' action becomes full width.
The booking proposition includes useful operational signals such as guest count, date, duration, departure, local experience, availability and skipper inclusion.
The visual system is clean and controlled overall, with good contrast, no horizontal overflow, and an accessible structural baseline.

aiReview.summary: This is a visually strong, technically polished luxury shell, but it is not yet reference-quality for premium Marbella real estate because the first viewport makes the buyer's next step ambiguous and hides too much of the property and supporting proposition. Clarifying the hero action, restoring image detail, and surfacing credible local expertise and search intent would materially improve enquiry conversion without sacrificing the editorial character.
strengths: The full-bleed villa photography, restrained palette, minimal chrome and centered wordmark create a convincingly aspirational premium-real-estate first impression.
Desktop and mobile preserve a coherent art direction rather than collapsing into a generic responsive layout; the mobile image crop remains intentional and the key controls stay visible.

The scan indicates a technically disciplined foundation: fast loading, no layout shift, no horizontal overflow, complete image alt coverage, valid page hierarchy, functional forms and no observed console or network failures.
The information architecture covers the right commercial territory, including properties, developments, areas, selling, insights and direct advisor contact.

aiReview.summary: La Bocana has a strong visual foundation and a credible Puerto Banus premium-restaurant identity, with excellent operational quality beneath it. It is not reference quality yet because the first conversion moment is visibly ceded to an oversized privacy panel, while the hero prioritizes generic luxury-terrrace atmosphere over culinary desire. Tightening the consent treatment, introducing a decisive food signal, and simplifying header hierarchy would materially improve perceived value and reservation readiness.
strengths: The hero photography, restrained serif/sans pairing, coastal palette, and waterfront context create a convincing premium Mediterranean atmosphere.
Location is explicit in the hero, and reservation is highly visible in both desktop and mobile navigation.
The information architecture is broadly appropriate for discovery: menu, house/story, gallery, contact and reservation are all available.

The supplied objective scan indicates a notably solid execution baseline: fast load performance, no layout shift, no horizontal overflow, accessible image alt coverage, working internal links, and no console or failed-network errors.
The "Best of the Best 2025" signal visible on mobile provides useful third-party credibility, although it is not given equal emphasis in the desktop first view.

issues.expected: Reference-quality premium real-estate design uses confident hierarchy and carefully art-directed, high-resolution photography of actual homes and places. Visual restraint should create focus, never conceal the product.
issues.observed: The page has no inspectable visual product and no perceived inventory value.
issues.recommendation: Replace the blocking screen with a composed property-first viewport: real hero/listing imagery with intentional crops, readable brand typography, restrained overlay treatment, and immediately visible browsing/contact controls. Keep any loader brief and non-blocking.
issues.title: The visual experience does not present a premium property product

issues.detail: The rendered document lacks meaningful content structure, including an H1 and headings, and exposes only three words. It cannot explain services, areas served, property types, or next steps.
issues.evidence: DOM scan reports `h1Count: 0`, no heading samples, `wordCount: 3`, and `documentOutlineOk: false`. No content is visible in either screenshot.
issues.expected: A real-estate homepage should have a clear semantic and visual hierarchy: agency/local proposition, property search or selected inventory, buyer/seller services, local expertise, and contact routes.
issues.observed: The site offers neither human-readable context nor a navigable information hierarchy.
issues.recommendation: Provide server-rendered or reliably rendered Spanish content with a single descriptive H1, supporting headings, concise service and locality copy, and navigable internal sections/pages. Do not rely on a loading layer to contain the primary page.
issues.title: No usable content hierarchy is rendered

issues.detail: The live state contains no visible legal/privacy access or trust material, which is particularly problematic where a property enquiry will collect personal data.
issues.evidence: The scan reports `hasPrivacyLink: false`, `hasLegalLink: false`, and `trustSignalCount: 0`. No footer or policy links are visible in the captures.
issues.expected: A credible Spanish property agency should visibly provide legal notice and privacy access, alongside concrete business identity and relevant trust indicators near contact capture and in the footer.
issues.location: Whole site, especially footer and future enquiry flow
issues.observed: There is no visible assurance around who operates the site or how enquiry data will be handled.
issues.recommendation: Add accessible footer links to Aviso legal, Política de privacidad, and cookie information where applicable; include verifiable agency identity, service area, and contact details. Place an appropriate privacy notice adjacent to every lead form.
issues.title: Trust and legal reassurance are missing

topPriority.title: No clear primary CTA was detected
topPriority.detail: The page does not expose a visible action matching common booking, reservation, enquiry, contact or purchase intent.
topPriority.recommendation: Define the page’s single primary conversion action and make it explicit in the hero/navigation with business-specific wording.
topPriority.expected: At least one obvious primary commercial action

aiReview.summary: This cannot currently be evaluated as a functioning premium real-estate website because both supplied viewports remain on a full-screen loading state. The unusually high automated visual and mobile scores are not credible proxies for the delivered customer experience: no inventory, imagery, hierarchy, local proof, navigation, or enquiry mechanism is available. Restoring reliable rendering is the prerequisite; only then can luxury art direction, property discovery, and lead conversion be meaningfully assessed.
strengths: The intended burgundy and gold palette could support a refined premium identity once it is applied to a functioning property-led experience.

Underlying technical measurements are strong: fast reported loading metrics, no console/network failures, no horizontal overflow, and sound baseline accessibility checks. These do not offset the visibly blocked rendered experience.
The supplied desktop and mobile frames are consistent in their failure state, making the core issue clear and reproducible across viewport classes.
